teaser: The most famous kiss in marble has not happened yet.

lesson.text: Her head has fallen back. Her arms have only just found the strength to rise. He has landed a second ago, wings still up, one knee on the rock, and he is bending down. Their lips are a finger's width apart. Antonio Canova stops the story right there, and it has stayed stopped since 1793.

So the title cheats a little. What you see is the breath before the kiss. Sculptors and painters had learned long ago that the instant just before an event holds more tension than the event itself, because your mind finishes the movement. Canova builds a whole marble around a gap.

The tale comes from a Roman novel written about 1,800 years ago. Psyche, a mortal girl, loves the god Cupid. His jealous mother Venus sends her to the underworld to fetch a sealed jar, with orders not to open it. She opens it. A deathlike sleep pours out and she drops to the ground. Cupid flies down to wake her.
In ancient Greek, “psyche” means both “soul” and “butterfly.” That is why Psyche often has butterfly wings in ancient art, and why the story was read for centuries as the soul being woken by love.

Two bodies and a pair of wings could easily turn into a tangle. Canova, a 30-year-old from the Venice region who was making his name in Rome, solved it with geometry. Seen from this side, the group is almost a diagram.
Three shapes hold the embrace together. They appear one at a time.

lines.label: First diagonal
lines.text: From the tip of one wing, through the two faces, down Psyche's body to her foot. A single sweep from the highest point of the group to its farthest edge.

lines.label: Second diagonal
lines.text: The other wing continues down Cupid's back and leg to his toes on the rock. Together the two lines make a large X, and the X crosses at the kiss.

lines.label: The ring
lines.text: Her raised arms and his encircling ones close into a loop around the two heads. Inside it there is only empty air and two faces. The frame is made of limbs.

lesson.text: An X to carry your eye in from the edges, a ring to keep it at the center. Canova makes a complicated embrace readable in one second.

The X only works from here, though. Walk a few steps and the lines shift: wings overlap, a quiver and the fatal jar appear on the far side. Some critics of the time complained that the group had no single correct view. Canova took that as a feature. He meant people to circle it, and he made that easy.

The pose was borrowed from a much older picture. Canova had seen a Roman wall painting dug up at Herculaneum, the town buried with Pompeii, showing a faun leaning over a reclining woman. He turned a flat, rather rowdy scene into a tender one in the round.

Then there is the surface. Canova's assistants roughed out the block from his full-size plaster model, measuring point by point. The final layer he kept for himself. He worked the skin with finer and finer tools, often by candlelight, because a low flame shows every bump. Different textures tell flesh from feather from stone.

spots.title: The gap
spots.text: Cupid's face tilts down, hers tilts up, and the mouths do not touch. Her eyes are still closed. She is waking into the kiss, not answering it yet.

spots.title: A hand under her head
spots.text: His fingers spread behind her neck and hair and take the weight of her head. Without this support she would fall back onto the rock.

spots.title: The other hand
spots.text: His second arm wraps her chest, fingers pressing lightly into her side. The marble seems to give under the fingertips, as soft as skin.

spots.title: Wings
spots.text: The feathers are thin enough at the edges for light to pass through the stone. They are still raised from the landing, which tells you he arrived a moment ago.

spots.title: The cloth
spots.text: A sheet slides off her hips in fine parallel creases. Its ripples make the smooth skin next to it look even smoother.

spots.title: Toes on the rock
spots.text: His foot pushes off a boulder that Canova left pitted and rough. The coarse stone is there for contrast: it is the only thing in the group that looks like rock.

lesson.text: That polish made Canova's reputation, and also some enemies. Admirers said his marble looked like living flesh. Others found it too sweet, too soft. He is reported to have toned down the raw white of new marble with a thin wash, so the skin would look warm and not like chalk.

A sculpture this suited to walking around needs space, and a patient owner. It was ordered in 1787 by a young British traveler, John Campbell, who never got it home. Around 1800 Joachim Murat, a general and Napoleon's brother-in-law, bought it for his house near Paris. And remember that Canova made circling the group easy. One small thing in the photo shows how.
The group was built to be turned so that viewers could see every side without moving. Find the tool for turning it.

spots.title: The handle
spots.text: A dark metal handle sticks out of the base beyond Psyche's foot. The marble once sat on a pivot, and an attendant could swing the whole group around like a slow carousel.

lesson.text: The novelist Gustave Flaubert met a version of this group at a villa on Lake Como in 1845, when he was 23. He wrote that he looked around, saw nobody was watching, and kissed the marble Psyche under her raised arm.

The group has been in the Louvre since the 1820s, and it no longer turns. A second version, carved for a Russian prince, is in St. Petersburg. Visitors now do the walking themselves, the way those critics said they would have to. From every side the lips stay the same distance apart.

quiz.question: What exact moment does Canova show?
options: The instant just before the kiss
The couple flying up to the gods
quiz.explanation: The lips are close but do not touch.

quiz.question: Why is Psyche unconscious?
options: She opened a jar that released a deathlike sleep
Cupid shot her with an arrow by mistake
quiz.explanation: She disobeyed Venus and opened the jar from the underworld.

quiz.question: Which shape do the wings and bodies form from this side?
quiz.explanation: Two diagonals cross at the faces.

quiz.question: What is the metal handle in the base for?
quiz.explanation: The group sat on a pivot so it could be turned for viewers.

quiz.question: What do the two meanings of the Greek word “psyche” have in common with this story?
quiz.explanation: Psyche means soul and butterfly, so the tale was read as love waking the soul.

quiz.question: Why did Canova like to finish his marbles by candlelight?
options: A low flame reveals every bump on the surface
He worked in secret at night
quiz.explanation: Raking light from a candle shows the smallest unevenness.

facts.text: In the sculpture, Cupid and Psyche's lips are touching.
facts.explanation: Canova freezes the moment just before the kiss.

facts.text: Canova took the pose from an ancient Roman wall painting.
facts.explanation: He adapted a painting of a faun and a woman found at Herculaneum.

facts.text: The British traveler who ordered the group displayed it in his home for decades.
facts.explanation: John Campbell never got it home, and it was later bought by Joachim Murat.
